lesson.title: The Segment: TCP's Unit of Delivery
lesson.summary: A TCP segment is TCP's protocol data unit, a chunk of a continuous byte stream wrapped in a header that carries the sequence numbers, acknowledgments, flags, and window size TCP needs to manage a connection.
lesson.body:
A segment, generically, is the unit a protocol hands down to the layer below it, and a TCP segment is what TCP calls that unit for itself, playing the same structural role that a datagram plays for UDP, but carrying far more bookkeeping, because a TCP segment has to help manage an entire ongoing connection rather than just deliver one isolated message.

An important distinction follows directly from that: TCP does not preserve application message boundaries the way a UDP datagram preserves the boundary of whatever the application handed to it. TCP treats everything an application writes as one continuous stream of bytes and is free to carve that stream into segments however is convenient at the moment, based on the receiver's advertised window, the sender's own buffering, the path's maximum transmission unit, and more. A single application write can end up split across two segments, or two separate writes can end up combined into one segment, and TCP is under no obligation to keep them separate. This is exactly why, as the next chapter explains, TCP counts bytes rather than counting segments or messages.

The TCP header carries source and destination port fields just like UDP does, but adds much more: a 32 bit sequence number, a 32 bit acknowledgment number, a data offset field recording the header's own length, a set of control flags including URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, and FIN, the last three of which drive the handshake and termination processes covered in the next two chapters, a 16 bit window size field central to flow control, a checksum, an urgent pointer, and optional fields. All of that brings the minimum header size, with no options, to 20 bytes, compared to UDP's flat 8 bytes. That gap in header size is, quite literally, the price of everything extra TCP does.

Consider a web server sending a 3,000 byte HTTP response over a connection where the usable payload per segment is limited to roughly 1,460 bytes by the path's maximum transmission unit. That 3,000 byte response cannot travel as one segment, it has to be split into three: two segments of about 1,460 bytes each and a final segment carrying the remaining 80 bytes. Each of those three pieces is wrapped in its own 20 byte TCP header, each header carries the sequence number marking exactly where that piece's data begins in the original 3,000 byte stream, and that sequence numbering is what lets the receiving browser reassemble the three pieces back into the correct 3,000 byte response even if the network happens to deliver them out of order.
